docs.title: Cell Phones for Soldiers
docs.text:
Computers West sponsors Cell Phones for Soldiers. Each contribution to Cell Phones For Soldiers provides military members with precious talk time through our Minutes That Matter program, and it gives each qualified veteran a cellular device to assist with employment, contacting loved ones and communicating with veteran resources.

Cell Phones for Soldiers was started by Brittany and Robbie Bergquist in 2004 when they heard of a soldier having a high phone bill from calling home. What started with raiding their piggy banks has grown into a nationwide cause. Our quest continues. Continue donating your old phones and pass the word! It’s one way to say Thank You to the men and women who continue to give so much to our country.

Our Cell Phones for Soldiers box is in the main room by the printer.

docs.title: History of Computers West
docs.text:
Computers West began in 1984 when seven Sun City West residents organized a club to help seniors learn emerging computer technology. Monthly meetings, user groups, and classes quickly followed as membership grew (over 2,700 by 2001).

Through the years, the club:

  • Established permanent facilities across Rec Centers, ultimately moving to Palm Ridge.
  • Ran free/low‑cost lectures and hands‑on classes (dozens per year).
  • Operated a Help Group that has saved members significant repair costs.
  • Donated equipment and supported local schools, hospitals, food banks, and programs such as Students Recycling Used Technology (RUT).
  • Collected thousands of devices for Cell Phones for Soldiers and other community drives.

The club remains true to its purpose: “Technology Has No Age Limit.”

Computers West provides a number of Special Interest groups (SIGs).

SIGs are self-organizing groups focused on specific topics, technologies, or activities.

docs.title: Streaming & Cord‑Cutting SIG
docs.text: Learn how to replace or augment traditional TV service with streaming, over‑the‑air reception, and simple home setups. This SIG covers device choices, service options, antenna basics, privacy and cost‑saving tips.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This Special Interest Group (SIG) helps members choose and configure streaming devices and services, combine them with free over‑the‑air (OTA) TV where appropriate, and troubleshoot common issues like buffering, account management, and smart TV settings.

What we cover

  • Choosing streaming devices: Roku, Apple TV, Amazon Fire TV, Android TV / Google TV, Chromecast.
  • Streaming services: free ad‑supported and paid subscription options.
  • OTA TV: antennas, tuners, and DVR options.
  • Network basics: Wi‑Fi setup, Ethernet, router placement, and QoS.
  • Privacy & security tips for streaming devices and accounts.

docs.title: SIG Meetings
docs.text:
• Regular meeting times and location are listed on the club calendar. Check the club site or SIG board for the next session and presentation topic.
  • Meetings typically include demonstrations, member Q&A, and hands‑on help.

docs.title: Streaming players
docs.text:
• Roku: simple interface, broad app support, good for users wanting minimal setup.
  • Amazon Fire TV: tight Amazon integration, good for Prime customers.
  • Apple TV: best for Apple ecosystem users; supports AirPlay.
  • Android TV / Google TV: integrates with Google services and Chromecast.
  • Chromecast: lightweight option for casting from phones and Chrome browser.

docs.title: Smart TVs
docs.text:
• Many smart TVs have built‑in platforms; evaluate app availability and update policy before buying.
  • Consider using an external streaming stick/player to avoid manufacturer bloatware and for more consistent updates.

docs.title: Antennas & OTA
docs.text:
• Use an indoor or outdoor antenna with adequate gain for your area. AntennaWeb or FCC TV Reception Maps help determine signal strength.
  • Tuners and OTA DVRs (e.g., Tablo, HDHomeRun) allow recording and streaming across home devices.

docs.title: Free options
docs.text:
• Free ad‑supported streaming (FAST) services: Pluto TV, Tubi, Peacock (free tier), Crackle, etc.
  • Network apps may offer free episodes or limited streaming.

docs.title: Paid subscriptions
docs.text:
• Streaming services: Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, Max, Paramount+, Apple TV+.
  • Consider rotating subscriptions and shared profiles to manage cost.

docs.title: Add‑ons & niche services
docs.text: • Sports packages, premium channels, and specialty apps are available à la carte.

docs.title: Network & Performance Tips
docs.text:
• Prefer wired Ethernet for primary streaming devices when possible.
  • For Wi‑Fi: place the router centrally, use 5 GHz for device support, and minimize interference.
  • If many devices stream simultaneously, consider upgrading bandwidth or enabling router QoS.
  • Clear app caches and keep device firmware updated to reduce performance issues.

docs.title: Setup Checklist
docs.text:
1. Choose a primary streaming device or smart TV.
  2. Confirm required apps/services are available on that device.
  3. Measure Wi‑Fi signal or connect via Ethernet.
  4. For OTA TV: check antenna direction, mounting height, and use a signal amplifier if needed.
  5. Create or sign in to streaming accounts and set up parental controls as needed.
  6. Test playback and adjust picture/HDMI settings for best quality.

docs.title: Privacy \& Account Safety
docs.text:
• Use strong, unique passwords and enable two‑factor authentication when available.
  • Review device privacy settings (voice assistants, viewing history, ad personalization).
  • Be cautious when granting app permissions.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Reboot modem/router and streaming device as a first step.
  • Check for outages with your ISP or with a specific streaming service.
  • Reduce stream quality temporarily if buffering persists.
  • Update the app and device firmware; reinstall the app if problems persist.

docs.title: 3D Scanning and Reverse Engineering
docs.text: This class introduces ways to capture or recreate real-world objects for 3D printing, along with the practical limits of scanning.

docs.title: Class Materials
docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • The difference between scanning an object and designing a replacement part.
  • Common capture methods: phone scanning, photogrammetry, and dedicated scanners.
  • Why scans often need cleanup before printing.
  • Why reverse engineering functional parts usually requires measurements.
  • When scanning is useful and when CAD is better.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Show a scanned decorative object or a phone-scanning workflow if available. Then compare it with measuring a simple functional part using calipers to explain why scanning is not always enough.

docs.title: 3D Scanning and Reverse Engineering: Attendee Handout
Scanning Works Best For
docs.text:
• Decorative objects.
  • Organic shapes.
  • Objects where exact dimensions are not critical.
  • Reference geometry for a new design.

docs.title: Scanning Works Poorly For
docs.text:
• Shiny objects.
  • Transparent objects.
  • Very dark objects.
  • Thin edges.
  • Precision mechanical parts.
  • Parts with hidden internal features.

docs.title: Reverse Engineering Workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify what the part must do.
  2. Measure key dimensions with calipers.
  3. Sketch the functional features.
  4. Model the part in CAD.
  5. Print a small fit test.
  6. Revise before printing the final part.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text: A scan gives you shape. A replacement part needs function, fit, material, and strength.

docs.title: Instructor Guide: 3D Scanning and Reverse Engineering
Audience
docs.text: Attendees who want to duplicate or adapt real-world objects.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• Scanning captures shape, but not design intent.
  • Decorative objects are usually better scanning candidates than precise mechanical parts.
  • Shiny, transparent, dark, thin, or featureless objects are hard to scan.
  • Mesh cleanup is often required before slicing.
  • Functional reverse engineering usually combines measurement, sketching, and CAD.
  • Copyright and ownership can matter when copying objects.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Explain scanning versus reverse engineering.
  2. Show examples of good and bad scan candidates.
  3. Demonstrate a scan viewer or short phone-scanning example if available.
  4. Show mesh problems: holes, rough surfaces, extra background geometry.
  5. Measure a simple object with calipers.
  6. Explain when to model from measurements instead of scanning.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: Can I scan a broken part and print a new one? Sometimes, but exact functional parts usually need measurements and CAD cleanup. Can a phone scan make printable files? Sometimes for decorative shapes, but quality varies and cleanup may be needed. Why does the scan look rough? Lighting, surface finish, camera movement, software, and object shape all affect results.

docs.title: AI Design
docs.text: This class explains practical ways AI can assist 3D printing projects, while setting realistic expectations about what AI can and cannot produce.

docs.title: Class Materials
docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • How AI can help brainstorm project ideas and requirements.
  • How AI can help write simple OpenSCAD or CAD-style instructions.
  • How image generation can help with visual concepts but not final printable engineering.
  • Why AI output must be checked for dimensions, strength, fit, and printability.
  • How to write prompts that include measurements and constraints.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Ask AI for a simple OpenSCAD model, such as a labeled cable tag or spacer with a hole. Review the generated code, identify assumptions, and explain what must be checked before printing.

docs.title: Good AI Uses
docs.text:
• Brainstorming project ideas.
  • Making a checklist of measurements.
  • Explaining CAD concepts.
  • Drafting simple OpenSCAD code.
  • Comparing material options.
  • Reviewing whether a design may be hard to print.

docs.title: Poor AI Uses
docs.text:
• Safety-critical parts.
  • Load-bearing parts without engineering review.
  • Exact-fit replacement parts without measurement and testing.
  • Assuming a generated visual image is printable.

docs.title: Prompt Checklist
docs.text:
Include:

  • What the part is for.
  • Key measurements in millimeters.
  • Material.
  • Printer type.
  • Strength or flexibility needs.
  • Whether supports should be avoided.
  • Any holes, clearances, or mounting points.

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: Treat AI output as a draft. Measure, inspect, slice, and test before relying on it.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Attendees who are curious about using AI to support 3D printing design work.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• AI is useful for brainstorming, checklists, simple scripts, and explaining CAD concepts.
  • AI should not be trusted blindly for load-bearing parts, safety-critical parts, or exact fit.
  • Good prompts include measurements, use case, material, printer limits, and constraints.
  • Generated files still need human review in CAD and slicer software.
  • AI-generated visual concepts are not the same as printable models.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Start with a practical problem.
  2. Prompt AI for design requirements and measurements to collect.
  3. Prompt AI for a simple OpenSCAD example.
  4. Review the code or dimensions.
  5. Explain what could be wrong.
  6. Show the model in a CAD viewer or slicer if available.

docs.title: Example Prompt
docs.text: Create a simple OpenSCAD model for a rectangular cable label tag. It should be 50 mm long, 18 mm wide, 2 mm thick, with a 4 mm zip-tie hole near each end. Use rounded corners if practical. Keep the design easy to print flat on an FDM printer.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: Can AI make STL files? Some tools can generate models, but results still need careful checking. Can AI replace CAD? Not for reliable functional work. It can help you start faster and learn concepts.

docs.title: Common Problems and Solutions
docs.text: This class covers the most common 3D printing problems beginners encounter and gives practical first steps for diagnosing and fixing them.

docs.title: Class Materials
docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • How to describe a print problem clearly.
  • Why first-layer problems are so common.
  • How bed adhesion, temperature, speed, moisture, and slicer settings affect results.
  • What to check before changing hardware.
  • How to change one variable at a time.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Show photos or physical examples of failed prints: poor first layer, warping, stringing, blobs, layer shift, clogged nozzle, and weak part. For each one, identify likely causes and first fixes.

docs.title: Common Problems and Solutions: Attendee Handout
First Rule
docs.text: Change one thing at a time. If you change five settings at once, you will not know what helped.

docs.title: Quick Checks
docs.text:
• Is the build plate clean?
  • Is the correct filament selected in the slicer?
  • Is the first layer smooth and attached?
  • Is the filament dry?
  • Is the model oriented correctly?
  • Does preview mode show supports and walls correctly?
  • Is the printer making unusual noises?

docs.title: Common Symptoms
docs.text: Poor first layer Clean the plate, check Z offset, check bed temperature, slow the first layer. Warped corners Add brim, avoid drafts, use correct bed temperature, consider another material. Stringing Dry filament, lower temperature, check retraction. Blobs or zits Check temperature, seam position, retraction, and filament moisture. Layer shift Check belts, pulleys, collisions, and print speed. Weak part Improve orientation, add walls, increase temperature if layers are not bonding, choose better material.

docs.title: Instructor Guide: Common Problems and Solutions
Audience
docs.text: Beginners who have printed at least once or who want to understand why prints fail.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• A good diagnosis starts with observing the print, not guessing.
  • The first layer affects the rest of the print.
  • Bed cleanliness, Z offset, temperature, and filament condition cause many problems.
  • Slicer preview can catch support, orientation, and thin-wall issues before printing.
  • Change one variable at a time or you will not know what fixed the problem.

docs.title: Problem Categories
docs.text: Poor bed adhesion Clean build plate, correct Z offset, correct bed temperature, brim if needed. Stringing Dry filament, temperature tuning, retraction settings, travel speed. Warping Material choice, bed temperature, enclosure, brim, avoid drafts. Layer shift Check belts, collisions, loose pulleys, speed, and mechanical obstruction. Clogged nozzle Check filament path, nozzle temperature, debris, heat creep, and nozzle condition. Weak parts Check orientation, walls, material, temperature, and layer adhesion.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Show a failed print or photo.
  2. Ask attendees what they observe.
  3. Name the symptom.
  4. List likely causes.
  5. Choose the first safe fix.
  6. Explain what not to change yet.

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • Why orientation affects strength, appearance, and support needs.
  • How overhangs, bridges, walls, and tolerances affect printability.
  • Why 3D printed parts are often weaker between layers.
  • How to design parts that need fewer supports.
  • How to plan small test prints before committing to a final design.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Show the same simple bracket or hook in two orientations. Compare support material, print time, layer direction, and likely strength.

docs.title: Design Checklist
docs.text:
• Can the part print without supports?
  • Is the strongest direction aligned with the load?
  • Are walls thick enough?
  • Do holes and slots have clearance?
  • Can the part be split into simpler pieces?
  • Is a small test print possible?

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: Overhang Part of a model that extends outward without material below it. Bridge A short span printed across a gap. Tolerance Extra space added so parts fit together after printing. Layer direction The direction layers are stacked; parts are often weakest between layers.

docs.title: Practical Advice
docs.text: Design for the printer you have, not the perfect printer you wish you had.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Attendees who want to create or modify models that print reliably.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• FDM parts are anisotropic: strength varies by direction.
  • Avoid steep unsupported overhangs where practical.
  • Split complicated parts if that makes printing easier.
  • Add chamfers or fillets carefully; they can help or hurt depending on orientation.
  • Holes, pegs, and snap fits need clearance.
  • Test coupons are faster than full-size failed prints.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Show a part with an obvious overhang.
  2. Slice it in the default orientation.
  3. Rotate it to reduce supports.
  4. Compare print time, supports, and surface quality.
  5. Discuss layer direction and likely failure direction.
  6. Show a small tolerance test or clearance example.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: How steep can an overhang be? Many printers handle about 45 degrees, but printer, material, cooling, and speed matter. Why are holes too tight? Plastic extrusion has width, and printers are not perfect. Holes often need clearance or calibration. Should I use supports? Use them when needed, but design and orient parts to avoid them when practical.

docs.title: Functional Parts and Repairs
docs.text: This class focuses on practical 3D printing for household fixes, brackets, clips, spacers, organizers, and replacement parts.

docs.title: Class Materials
docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • How to decide whether a repair part is a good 3D printing candidate.
  • How to measure an existing object with calipers.
  • How material, orientation, and wall count affect functional parts.
  • Why prototypes and fit tests are important.
  • When not to use a printed part for safety reasons.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Measure a simple object such as a drawer spacer, knob, clip, or bracket. Sketch the important dimensions and discuss how it would be modeled, printed, tested, and revised.

docs.title: Functional Parts and Repairs: Attendee Handout
Good Candidates
docs.text:
• Spacers
  • Cable guides
  • Drawer organizers
  • Light-duty brackets
  • Knobs
  • Feet and bumpers
  • Covers and caps
  • Templates and jigs

docs.title: Poor Candidates
docs.text:
• High-heat parts near engines, ovens, or lamps.
  • Safety-critical parts.
  • Parts that hold people, pets, vehicles, or heavy loads.
  • Food-contact parts unless material and process are appropriate.

docs.title: Measurement Checklist
docs.text:
• Overall length, width, and height.
  • Hole diameter and spacing.
  • Wall thickness.
  • Clearance needed for movement.
  • Load direction.
  • Temperature and environment.

docs.title: Repair Workflow
docs.text:
1. Understand the function.
  2. Measure the key features.
  3. Choose material.
  4. Design or customize the part.
  5. Print a small test.
  6. Adjust and print final version.

docs.title: Instructor Guide: Functional Parts and Repairs
Audience
docs.text: Attendees interested in practical repairs and utility parts rather than decorative prints.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• Not every broken part should be replaced with plastic.
  • Measure the job the part must do, not just the old part's shape.
  • Calipers are essential for fit.
  • Functional parts usually need attention to orientation, walls, and material.
  • Small test pieces reduce wasted time.
  • Avoid safety-critical uses unless the design is properly engineered.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Present a broken or missing part.
  2. Identify the function: hold, space, guide, cover, label, grip, or adapt.
  3. Measure key dimensions with calipers.
  4. Sketch the part and mark tolerances.
  5. Discuss material choice.
  6. Discuss print orientation for strength.
  7. Plan a fit test.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: Can 3D printed parts replace metal? Sometimes for light-duty uses, but not automatically. Load, heat, wear, and safety matter. How accurate are printed parts? Accuracy depends on printer calibration, material, orientation, and design clearance. What should I print first? A small fit test or critical feature, not the entire final part.

docs.title: Getting Models
docs.text: This class explains where 3D models come from, how to evaluate them before printing, and how to avoid common problems with downloaded files. It is designed for a presentation and short live demonstration that fits within 45 minutes.

docs.title: Class Materials
docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • Where to find printable 3D models.
  • The difference between STL, 3MF, and source design files.
  • How licenses affect personal use, sharing, remixing, and selling.
  • How to judge whether a model is likely to print successfully.
  • When to use a downloaded model, customize one, or design from scratch.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Open a model site such as Printables, Thingiverse, MakerWorld, or MyMiniFactory. Choose one simple functional item and one decorative item, then compare file formats, photos, print settings, license, comments, and remix/customization options.

docs.title: Good Places To Look
docs.text:
• Printables
  • MakerWorld
  • Thingiverse
  • MyMiniFactory
  • Thangs
  • Cults, when the license and source are acceptable

docs.title: Before Downloading
docs.text:
Check:

  • Photos of real prints, not only computer renderings.
  • File type: STL, 3MF, or source file.
  • License and allowed use.
  • Whether supports are needed.
  • Recommended material and print settings.
  • Comments from people who already printed it.
  • Whether the model is the right size for your printer.

docs.title: Useful Terms
docs.text: STL A common mesh file format that stores the model shape. 3MF A newer format that can store model and project information. Remix A modified version of someone else's model. License Rules that explain how the model may be used, changed, or shared.

docs.title: Practical Advice
docs.text: Start with small, proven models. A simple successful print teaches more than a large failed one.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Beginners who understand the basic 3D printing workflow but do not yet know how to find or evaluate models.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• A printer does not create the object by itself; it needs a digital model.
  • STL files describe shape only. 3MF files can include additional project information.
  • Source files such as Fusion, Onshape, Blender, or OpenSCAD files are better for editing.
  • Download popularity is useful, but photos, comments, and print examples matter more.
  • Licenses vary. Personal use, remixing, attribution, and commercial use are not the same thing.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Open a model repository.
  2. Search for a simple practical object such as a cable clip, hook, or spacer.
  3. Review photos, model description, print orientation, supports, and comments.
  4. Open the license and explain what it permits.
  5. Download the file or show where the file would be downloaded.
  6. Open the file in a slicer and inspect its size and orientation.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: What site is best? No single site is best. Printables, MakerWorld, Thingiverse, MyMiniFactory, and other libraries each have strengths. Can I sell something I downloaded? Only if the license allows it. Many models are personal-use only or require attribution. Why did a downloaded model fail? The model may require a different printer, material, orientation, support strategy, or scale.

docs.title: Instructor Notes
docs.text: Avoid turning this class into a long tour of every model site. The useful skill is evaluating a model before spending time and filament on it.

docs.title: Maintenance and Calibration
docs.text: This class introduces routine printer care and basic calibration checks that help keep prints reliable.

docs.title: Class Materials
docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • What routine maintenance tasks are safe for beginners.
  • Why cleaning the build plate matters.
  • How belts, nozzles, filament path, and lubrication affect print quality.
  • What calibration prints can and cannot tell you.
  • Why printer-specific manuals and maintenance logs matter.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Show a basic maintenance checklist and physical examples if available: clean build plate, nozzle, filament path, belt tension check, and a simple calibration print such as a temperature tower or flow test.

docs.title: Routine Checks
docs.text:
• Clean build plate.
  • Inspect nozzle for buildup.
  • Check filament path.
  • Listen for unusual noises.
  • Check belts for obvious looseness or damage.
  • Keep rods, screws, or rails maintained according to the printer manual.
  • Remove loose filament scraps from the printer.

docs.title: Calibration Prints
docs.text: First-layer test Checks bed adhesion and nozzle distance. Temperature tower Helps compare print quality at different temperatures. Flow test Helps tune extrusion amount for a filament. Retraction test Helps reduce stringing.

docs.title: Maintenance Log
docs.text:
Record:

  • Date.
  • Filament used.
  • Problem noticed.
  • Change made.
  • Result.

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: Do not adjust random settings because a print failed. Identify the symptom first.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Printer owners or prospective owners who want reliable prints without over-adjusting the machine.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• Maintenance prevents many print problems.
  • Cleaning the build plate is simple and high impact.
  • Nozzle, extruder, belts, rods, screws, fans, and filament path all matter.
  • Calibration should be done intentionally, not randomly.
  • Automated calibration helps but does not replace inspection.
  • Keep a simple maintenance log.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Show a printer maintenance checklist.
  2. Demonstrate build plate cleaning method appropriate to the plate.
  3. Point out nozzle, extruder, belts, rods, fans, and filament path.
  4. Show examples of dirty nozzle or worn filament path if available.
  5. Explain temperature tower, flow test, and first-layer test.
  6. Discuss when to stop and consult printer-specific documentation.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: How often should I clean the plate? Whenever adhesion declines or after touching the surface. Oils from fingers can cause failures. Should I adjust belts often? No. Check them when symptoms suggest a problem or when the printer manual recommends it. Do I need to calibrate everything? No. Start with known profiles and calibrate when there is a specific reason.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: This class introduces common 3D printing materials, what they are good for, and what safety or printer requirements they may have.

docs.title: Class Materials
docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • Why PLA is usually the easiest starting material.
  • When PETG, TPU, ABS, ASA, resin, or specialty materials may be useful.
  • How heat, flexibility, sunlight, strength, detail, and safety affect material choice.
  • Why some materials require ventilation, enclosures, drying, or services.
  • How filament storage affects print quality.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Show physical samples of PLA, PETG, TPU, silk PLA, wood-filled PLA, and a failed wet-filament print if available. Compare stiffness, surface finish, flexibility, and intended use.

docs.title: Common Materials
docs.text: PLA Easiest beginner material. Good for indoor decorative and light functional prints. PETG Tougher than PLA and more heat resistant. Good for many practical parts. TPU Flexible material for bumpers, feet, grips, and soft parts. ABS / ASA Stronger heat-resistant materials, but often require enclosure and ventilation. Resin High detail, but requires chemical handling, washing, curing, gloves, and disposal care. Specialty filaments Silk, wood-filled, carbon fiber-filled, glow, metal-filled, and other blends may need special settings or hardened nozzles.

docs.title: Selection Questions
docs.text:
• Will the part be indoors or outdoors?
  • Will it get hot?
  • Does it need to bend?
  • Does it need to hold weight?
  • Does appearance matter more than strength?
  • Is the material safe and practical for the available printer?

docs.title: Storage Tip
docs.text: Keep filament dry and sealed when not in use, especially PETG, TPU, nylon, and many specialty materials.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Beginners and intermediate users who need help choosing material for a project.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• Material choice should follow the use case.
  • PLA is easy and good for many indoor decorative and light-duty parts.
  • PETG is tougher and more heat resistant than PLA, but can be stringier.
  • TPU is flexible and useful for grips, bumpers, and soft parts.
  • ABS and ASA can be useful but usually require enclosure and ventilation.
  • Resin can produce fine detail but requires chemical handling and post-processing.
  • Specialty filaments can be abrasive, brittle, expensive, or harder to print.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Show a simple comparison table.
  2. Pass around or display labeled material samples.
  3. Match sample objects to use cases.
  4. Explain storage and moisture problems.
  5. Discuss safety and ventilation at a high level.
  6. Close with a material selection checklist.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: What material should beginners use? PLA, unless the part has a specific requirement PLA cannot meet. Can I print outdoor parts in PLA? Sometimes, but PETG or ASA may be better depending on heat, sun, and load. Do I need a filament dryer? Not always, but wet filament can cause poor surface finish, popping, stringing, and weak prints.

docs.title: Parametric Design
docs.text: This class introduces parametric design: creating models that can be adjusted by changing measurements instead of redrawing the object from scratch.

docs.title: Using OpenSCAD for Parametric Design
docs.text: OpenSCAD is a free, script‑based 3D modeling tool that excels at parametric geometry. It treats your model as code, so changing a variable automatically rebuilds the shape.

docs.title: What is OpenSCAD?
docs.text: OpenSCAD (https://openscad.org) is a 3‑D CAD program that lets you define objects using a simple programming language. Unlike most modeling tools, there is no interactive mouse editing; you edit the script and press Compile to see the result.

docs.title: Download & Install
docs.text:
• Windows: download the installer from the website and run it. It creates a openscad.exe in your Program Files.
  • macOS: use Homebrew with brew install --cask openscad or download the DMG from the site.
  • Linux: most distros ship a package; e.g., sudo apt install openscad.

docs.title: Example Script
docs.text:
// Simple adjustable box
module custom_box(width=20, height=10, depth=30, wall=2) {
    difference() {
        cube([width, height, depth]);
        translate([wall, wall, wall])
            cube([width-2*wall, height-2*wall, depth-2*wall]);
    }
}

custom_box(); // call with defaults

docs.title: Using the Customizer Window
docs.text:
OpenSCAD provides a Customizer panel that lets you tweak parameters interactively: 1. Open the script. 2. Click View → Customizer (or press Ctrl+Shift+C). 3. A sidebar appears with sliders for each parameter. 4. Adjust values and the preview updates instantly. 5. When satisfied, click Export to save an STL.

This workflow shows how a single script can generate many variations without requiring manual redesign.

docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • What parametric design means.
  • Why measurements and constraints matter.
  • How changing a value can resize or reshape a model.
  • Where parametric models are useful: boxes, brackets, organizers, adapters, and repair parts.
  • Why simple, well-named parameters are easier to maintain.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Use a simple customizable object such as a spacer, hook, label tag, or small box. Change width, height, hole size, and wall thickness, then export a new STL.

docs.title: What It Means
docs.text: Parametric design means the model is controlled by measurements. Instead of redrawing the object, you change values such as length, width, hole diameter, or wall thickness.

docs.title: Good Uses
docs.text:
• Spacers
  • Boxes
  • Brackets
  • Cable clips
  • Drawer organizers
  • Adapters
  • Replacement knobs or feet

docs.title: Useful Habits
docs.text:
• Measure with calipers.
  • Write down dimensions before modeling.
  • Name parameters clearly.
  • Change one parameter at a time.
  • Test with small prints before printing the final object.

docs.title: Why Not Just Scale?
docs.text: Scaling an STL changes every dimension. That can make screw holes, slots, and wall thickness wrong. Parametric changes are more controlled.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Attendees who want to customize objects but are not ready for a full CAD course.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• Parametric design uses named dimensions and relationships.
  • A small number of clear parameters is better than a complicated model.
  • Calipers are important because useful designs usually start with real measurements.
  • Constraints keep sketches predictable when dimensions change.
  • Parametric models are excellent for repeated variations.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Show the finished model first.
  2. Identify the measurements that should be adjustable.
  3. Change one parameter and regenerate the model.
  4. Show how a hole or slot changes with the parameter.
  5. Export the modified model.
  6. Open it in the slicer to confirm scale and shape.

docs.title: Tool Options
docs.text:
• OpenSCAD for text-based parametric models.
  • Tinkercad for simple visual edits.
  • Fusion or Onshape for sketch-based parametric CAD.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: Do I need to learn CAD? For serious custom parts, yes eventually. For simple parameter changes, many models can be customized without deep CAD knowledge. Why not just scale the STL? Scaling changes everything, including holes, walls, and fit. Parametric design changes the intended dimensions.

docs.title: Post Processing
docs.text: This class covers what happens after a print finishes: removing supports, cleaning up surfaces, joining parts, adding hardware, and finishing safely.

docs.title: Class Materials
docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • How to remove prints and supports without damaging the part.
  • Basic cleanup tools and safety precautions.
  • When sanding, filing, deburring, glue, or paint are useful.
  • How heat-set inserts and hardware can improve functional parts.
  • Why resin post-processing requires special safety steps.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Use a finished print with supports or rough edges. Demonstrate safe removal, light deburring, and how a heat-set insert or screw can be used in a printed part.

docs.title: Common Tasks
docs.text:
• Remove print from bed.
  • Remove supports.
  • Trim strings or blobs.
  • File or sand rough edges.
  • Glue parts together.
  • Add screws, magnets, or heat-set inserts.
  • Paint or label the print.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Wear eye protection when clipping supports.
  • Use gloves when appropriate.
  • Control sanding dust.
  • Be careful with blades and deburring tools.
  • Follow resin safety rules for uncured resin and wash liquid.

docs.title: Useful Tools
docs.text:
• Flush cutters
  • Deburring tool
  • Needle files
  • Sandpaper
  • Hobby knife
  • Small pliers
  • Soldering iron for heat-set inserts
  • Glue appropriate to the material

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Attendees who have printed objects and want them to look better or work better.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• Let the bed cool before forcing a print loose.
  • Support removal can damage small details if rushed.
  • Deburring tools, files, and sandpaper are useful but require care.
  • Dust and fumes should be managed safely.
  • Heat-set inserts can make stronger threaded connections.
  • Resin prints require gloves, washing, curing, and proper disposal.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Show a print fresh off the bed.
  2. Demonstrate safe part removal or explain bed cooling.
  3. Remove supports from a sample.
  4. Deburr a rough edge.
  5. Show sanding stages or finished examples.
  6. Demonstrate or describe heat-set inserts.
  7. Discuss paint, glue, and safety.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: Should I sand PLA? You can, but it takes patience. Start with coarse grit only when needed and work upward. What glue works? It depends on material. Cyanoacrylate works for many PLA parts; other materials may need different adhesives. Are resin prints safe after curing? Fully cured resin is safer to handle, but uncured resin and wash liquid require protective handling and proper disposal.

docs.title: Slicing
docs.text: This class introduces slicer software and the basic settings that turn a 3D model into printer instructions. It is designed around OrcaSlicer, but the concepts apply to most slicers.

docs.title: Class Materials
docs.text:
• Slide Deck
  • Instructor Guide
  • Attendee Handout
  • Timing Plan

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • What a slicer does.
  • Why printer, filament, and process profiles matter.
  • How layer height, walls, infill, supports, and orientation affect a print.
  • How to use preview mode before sending a job to the printer.
  • Why changing fewer settings is safer for beginners.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text: Load a simple model in OrcaSlicer. Show profile selection, orientation, supports, layer height, infill, slice preview, estimated time, and exported printer instructions.

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
1. Open the model.
  2. Choose the correct printer profile.
  3. Choose the correct filament profile.
  4. Choose a process or quality profile.
  5. Orient the model.
  6. Decide whether supports are needed.
  7. Slice the model.
  8. Review preview mode.
  9. Send or export the print job.

docs.title: Settings To Know
docs.text: Layer height Smaller layers can improve detail but increase print time. Walls Outer perimeters that often affect strength more than infill. Infill Internal structure that supports top layers and adds some strength. Supports Temporary material for steep overhangs. Brim Extra material around the base to improve bed adhesion.

docs.title: Beginner Rule
docs.text: Use a known-good profile, then change one thing at a time.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Beginners who have seen the 3D printing workflow and are ready to understand what happens inside the slicer.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• The slicer converts the model into layers and printer movements.
  • Profiles prevent many beginner mistakes by matching the printer and material.
  • Orientation can affect strength, surface quality, support need, and print time.
  • Preview mode is where many problems can be caught before printing.
  • More infill does not automatically mean a better part; walls often matter more.

docs.title: Demo Flow
docs.text:
1. Open OrcaSlicer.
  2. Select the printer, filament, and process profile.
  3. Import a simple model.
  4. Show move, rotate, scale, and lay-flat tools.
  5. Compare layer heights.
  6. Compare low and moderate infill.
  7. Turn supports on and off for an overhang example.
  8. Slice and inspect preview by layer.
  9. Show time and filament estimates.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text: Should I use default settings? Yes at first. Change one setting at a time after you understand the result. What infill should I use? Many decorative prints use low infill. Functional parts may need more walls, better orientation, or different material. Why does preview matter? Preview shows supports, gaps, thin walls, travel moves, and likely problem areas before material is wasted.

docs.title: Introduction to 3D Printing
docs.text: This class introduces the basic ideas, vocabulary, and workflow of 3D printing. It is designed as a short overview that can be presented in less than 45 minutes.

docs.text:
• Instructor Guide

docs.title: Class Goal
docs.text:
By the end of the class, attendees should understand:

  • What 3D printing is.
  • What kinds of things can be made with 3D printing.
  • How a digital 3D model becomes a physical object.
  • Why some people should use 3D printing services instead of owning a printer.
  • Why owning a printer can still be useful for frequent users and rapid prototyping.

docs.title: Suggested Demonstration
docs.text:
Use a simple STL model such as docs/sigs/3d-printing/example-models/3dbenchy.stl or another small model that loads quickly in OrcaSlicer.

Show the model, slice it, preview the generated toolpath, and explain that the printer follows the generated G-code instructions to create the physical object one layer at a time.

docs.title: What Is 3D Printing?
docs.text: 3D printing is a way to create physical objects from digital 3D models. Many beginner printers build objects one thin layer at a time.

docs.title: What Can You Make?
docs.text:
Functional examples:

  • Replacement parts.
  • Brackets, clips, mounts, and adapters.
  • Tools, jigs, and fixtures.
  • Prototypes to test fit, appearance, and function.

Decorative examples:

  • Figurines and display objects.
  • Ornaments and gifts.
  • Props and cosplay items.
  • Educational and architectural models.

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
1. Get or create a 3D model, often as an STL file.
  2. Open the model in slicer software such as OrcaSlicer.
  3. Choose printer, material, and print settings.
  4. Generate G-code.
  5. Transfer the file to the printer by Wi-Fi, USB, SD card, or another supported method.
  6. Print the object.
  7. Remove supports or clean up the print if needed.

docs.title: Useful Terms
docs.text: STL A common 3D model file format. Slicer Software that turns a model into printer instructions. G-code The instructions a printer follows to create the object. Layer height The thickness of each printed layer. Infill The internal structure of a print. Supports Temporary structures used to hold up overhanging parts during printing. FDM or FFF A common type of plastic 3D printing that melts filament. Resin printing A process that uses light to cure liquid resin.

docs.title: Reasons Not to Own a Printer
docs.text:
• Some materials require industrial printers.
  • Metal printing can require expensive equipment, special power, and fire suppression.
  • Resin and some other processes involve chemicals.
  • Some materials or processes can create fumes, particles, or toxic gases.
  • No single printer can print every material.
  • Printers require space, maintenance, calibration, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Reasons to Own a Printer
docs.text:
• You print often.
  • You want quick turnaround.
  • You want to make low-cost plastic test parts.
  • You want to revise designs quickly.
  • You want to validate fit, appearance, or function before ordering a specialty material from a service.

docs.title: Practical Beginner Advice
docs.text:
• Start with simple models.
  • PLA on an FDM printer is often the easiest place to begin.
  • Preview the sliced model before printing.
  • Watch the first layer of a print.
  • Expect occasional failed prints.
  • Use print services for materials such as tool steel, titanium, gold, ceramic, or other specialty materials.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Before Printing
docs.text:
• Does the object need to be strong, flexible, heat resistant, food safe, decorative, or precise?
  • What material is appropriate?
  • Is a home printer safe and practical for that material?
  • Would a print service be easier or less expensive?
  • Is a quick plastic prototype useful before ordering the final part?

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: This class is for beginners who are curious about 3D printing but may not own a printer or know the basic workflow. The goal is orientation, not hands-on mastery.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
Attendees should leave with a practical understanding of:

  • 3D printing as an additive manufacturing process.
  • Common uses for functional and decorative prints.
  • The basic workflow from STL model to slicer to G-code to printer.
  • The limits and risks of owning a 3D printer.
  • The reasons a personal 3D printer can still be valuable.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: 3D model A digital representation of an object. STL A common file format used to describe the shape of a 3D model. Slicer Software that turns a 3D model into printer instructions. This class uses OrcaSlicer as the example. G-code Instructions that tell the printer how to move, heat, extrude material, and build the object. FDM or FFF printer A common plastic 3D printer type that melts filament and deposits it layer by layer. Resin printer A printer that cures liquid resin with light. Resin printing can produce fine detail but requires more chemical handling. Print service A company, library, makerspace, or other organization that prints models for customers or members.

docs.title: 1. What Is 3D Printing?
docs.text:
Explain that 3D printing is a method of making physical objects from digital files. Most beginner printers build parts one thin layer at a time. This is different from cutting, drilling, or machining material away.

Keep the explanation simple:

  • A model describes the shape.
  • The slicer converts the shape into layers and machine instructions.
  • The printer follows those instructions to build the object.

docs.title: 2. What Can Be Done With 3D Printing?
docs.text:
Separate examples into two broad categories.

Functional models include:

  • Replacement knobs, brackets, clips, mounts, and adapters.
  • Prototypes used to test size, fit, and shape.
  • Tools, fixtures, jigs, organizers, and repair parts.
  • Enclosures for electronics or hobby projects.

Decorative models include:

  • Figurines, ornaments, display pieces, and art objects.
  • Cosplay pieces, props, and game accessories.
  • Gifts and personalized items.
  • Architectural or educational models.

Point out that many prints can be both functional and decorative.

docs.title: 3. Process Overview
docs.text:
Walk through the complete workflow:

  1. Start with a 3D model, commonly an STL file.
  2. Open the model in a slicer such as OrcaSlicer.
  3. Choose print settings such as material, layer height, infill, supports, and orientation.
  4. Generate G-code.
  5. Transfer the job to the printer by Wi-Fi, USB, SD card, or other supported method.
  6. Start the print and monitor the first layers.
  7. Remove the finished model and perform any cleanup.

If time allows, show a model in OrcaSlicer and switch to preview mode so attendees can see layers and toolpaths.

docs.title: 4. Why You Might Not Want to Own a Printer
docs.text:
Owning a printer is not the right answer for every person or every project.

Discuss these limitations:

  • Some materials, including many metals, require expensive industrial printers.
  • Industrial metal printing may require specialized power, ventilation, fire suppression, powder handling, or controlled environments.
  • Resin and some other processes involve chemicals that need careful handling, storage, gloves, cleaning, curing, and disposal.
  • Some materials or processes can create fumes, particulates, or toxic gases that many people do not want in a home.
  • No single printer can print every material that can be 3D printed.
  • Printers require maintenance, calibration, troubleshooting, and space.

Emphasize that print services can be the better choice when the material, safety requirements, or cost exceed what makes sense at home.

docs.title: 5. Why You May Want Your Own Printer
docs.text:
Owning a printer can be valuable when the person expects to print often or iterate quickly.

Use examples:

  • Printing frequent hobby, repair, or prototype parts.
  • Getting a quick turnaround without waiting for a service.
  • Testing fit, appearance, and function in inexpensive plastic.
  • Making several revisions before paying for an expensive material.
  • Validating a design at home before sending it to a service for tool steel, titanium, gold, ceramic, or another specialty material.

docs.title: 6. Closing
docs.text:
End with practical guidance:

  • Start with simple models and common materials.
  • PLA on an FDM printer is often the easiest entry point.
  • Expect some failed prints while learning.
  • Preview sliced models before printing.
  • Use services for specialty materials or safety-sensitive processes.

docs.title: Optional Demonstration Script
docs.text:
1. Open an STL file in OrcaSlicer.
  2. Rotate the model and identify the build plate.
  3. Show common settings: printer, filament, layer height, infill, supports.
  4. Click slice.
  5. Show the preview and explain the layer-by-layer toolpath.
  6. Explain that the G-code is transferred to the printer.
  7. If a printer is available, show the beginning of a print or a finished example.

docs.title: Instructor Notes
docs.text:
• Keep the technical vocabulary brief and repeat the core workflow several times.
  • Avoid turning this class into printer-buying advice unless attendees ask.
  • Bring a few example prints if possible: one functional part, one decorative part, and one failed print.
  • A failed print is useful because it sets realistic expectations.

docs.title: What is 3D printing?
docs.text: 3‑D printing, also known as additive manufacturing, builds objects layer by layer from digital models.

docs.title: What materials can be used?
docs.text: Common filaments include PLA, ABS, PETG, and TPU. Resin printers use liquid photopolymer resins.

docs.title: How do I choose a printer?
docs.text: Consider your budget, required resolution, build volume, and material compatibility.

docs.title: What is support structure?
docs.text: Supports are temporary scaffolds printed to hold overhanging parts; they are removed after printing.

docs.title: How do I prepare a model for printing?
docs.text: Use slicing software to generate G‑code, set layer height, infill, and support settings.

docs.title: FDM (Fused Deposition Modeling)
docs.text: A common 3‑D printing technology that extrudes melted thermoplastic filament layer by layer, building the part from the bottom up.

docs.title: SLA (Stereolithography)
docs.text: Uses a laser or light source to cure liquid resin into solid objects, offering high resolution and smooth surface finish.

docs.title: Print bed
docs.text: The build platform where the object is printed. It is often heated to reduce warping and improve adhesion.

docs.title: Layer height
docs.text: The vertical thickness of each printed layer. Smaller values increase resolution but also print time.

docs.title: Supports
docs.text: Temporary structures printed to support overhanging geometry. They are removed after printing.
